checkpoints: Identifies the core vulnerability: the origin VM still has a Public IP directly reachable, so requests that skip Front Door still reach the origin — meaning Front Door's WAF and caching only protect traffic that goes through it, while an attacker who knows the IP bypasses everything.

Layer one (identification): Front Door automatically stamps an X-Azure-FDID header on every request it forwards to the origin, and this header's value must match the Front Door profile's resource_guid — a value an attacker cannot fabricate since it's generated by that specific Front Door instance.

Layer two (enforcement): the origin (via NSG rule, firewall, or application middleware) must be configured to accept only requests satisfying both conditions simultaneously — originating from the AzureFrontDoor.Backend service tag AND carrying an FDID header matching the profile's resource_guid — rejecting everything else, even requests that know the origin IP.

On the Premium SKU, proposes Private Link as the stronger solution: connecting Front Door to the origin so the origin needs no Public IP at all, eliminating the direct-IP attack surface entirely instead of only blocking it via header/NSG checks.

On Standard SKU without Private Link, states that NSG service-tag filtering plus an application-level FDID check together form the required minimum, explaining that the service tag alone is insufficient because a different organization's Front Door instance shares the same AzureFrontDoor.Backend IP range and could call the origin directly — missing either check still leaves a bypass gap.

Core trade-off: all three tiers (Hot/Cool/Archive) sit on one axis balancing storage cost against access cost — the less frequently data is accessed, the lower the tier it should move to, saving on storage at the cost of paying more when it is occasionally read.

Hot tier has the highest storage cost but the lowest access cost, making it the right fit for the product images since the website reads them constantly and cheap reads matter more than cheap storage.
Cool tier is cheaper than Hot to store but pricier to read — fitting last month's logs, which are only occasionally looked up and don't need Hot-level read speed.
Cool tier carries a minimum storage duration (an early-deletion/tier-change penalty) — a structural cost distinct from the base storage/read price difference.

Archive tier is the cheapest to store, but the data sits offline and requires rehydration (a wait of hours) to read — a perfect fit for the legally-required 3-year quarterly backups that are almost never read again, since long-term storage cost dominates any concern about read speed.
Archive tier only accepts newly-written block blobs — a structural write-path constraint distinct from the storage/access cost trade-off, and a natural fit for write-once backup data.

Tiering can be set as a default at the storage-account level (overridable per individual blob), or automated entirely via a lifecycle-management policy that ages blobs down through the tiers over time.

The Terraform change `shared_access_key_enabled = false` disables access-key authentication entirely at the storage-account level — it removes that auth method as a valid option, not just restricts it.

The app code builds `BlobServiceClient.fromConnectionString` with a connection string containing `AccountKey=${accountKey}` — that is exactly access-key authentication, so once the flag takes effect every such request is now rejected.

The failure occurs at the authentication layer itself — Azure returns `403 AuthenticationFailed` in bulk because the app's auth method is no longer accepted, NOT because of a network error, RBAC permission issue, or firewall block.

Do not roll back to `shared_access_key_enabled = true` — that reverses the exact vulnerability the ops team was closing: an access key is a static secret easy to leak (git/logs), a leaked key grants full account access, and it has no easy rotation.
Correct fix — assign a Managed Identity to the compute running the app: system-assigned if the app runs on exactly one resource, user-assigned if the identity needs to be shared.
Grant the appropriate data-plane RBAC role to that identity on the storage account: `Storage Blob Data Contributor` if the app needs to write, `Storage Blob Data Reader` if read-only.
Rewrite the code to drop the key-bearing connection string entirely and use `DefaultAzureCredential` (SDK fetches a token via Managed Identity/IMDS automatically) passed into `BlobServiceClient`.

After the fix, re-test the real upload flow to confirm the 403 is gone, and grep the whole codebase for other places still using a connection string with `AccountKey` — an access key is often embedded in multiple places (background worker, CI script, another service), and all of them will fail the same way once shared key auth is off.

Chooses the vCore purchasing model over DTU, reasoning that DTU (Basic/S0/P2) bundles compute+storage+IO into a single number and doesn't give the fine-grained cost control the manager asked for, while vCore (GP_Gen5_2/BC_Gen5_2...) separates compute and storage pricing.
States that Azure Hybrid Benefit (setting license_type to reuse an already-owned SQL Server license) is only available on the vCore purchasing model, not on DTU.

Explains the resource structure: azurerm_mssql_server is just the logical/administrative endpoint (FQDN, admin login, firewall, Entra ID admin) with no compute of its own and is not a VM, while the vCore SKU and all compute/storage cost attach to azurerm_mssql_database.
Uses azurerm_mssql_failover_group to link the primary server with a partner server in a different region, declaring which databases replicate.
Notes that the failover group exposes a single read-write listener (FQDN shaped like <group>.database.windows.net) that the app connects to, rather than connecting directly to a server.

Explains failover behavior — automatic failover after a grace_minutes window, or a manually triggered failover — during which Azure repoints the listener's FQDN to the new primary so the app's connection string doesn't change.
Distinguishes the failover group from a read replica (read_scale — read-scaling only, same region, not DR).

Distinguishes the failover group from geo-restore (manual restore from backup, much larger RTO/RPO, no automatic failover), concluding the failover group is the genuine automatic cross-region DR mechanism for surviving a whole region going down.
Root cause is a hot partition, not insufficient overall RU/s — the container has RU/s to spare, but one physical partition is saturated

Cosmos hashes the partition key value to distribute documents across physical partitions, and each physical partition has its own hard cap (~10,000 RU/s and ~50GB) independent of the container's total provisioned throughput

/country has low, skewed cardinality — only a few dozen values, with a handful of large-market countries holding most customers — so the hash concentrates most documents/traffic onto one or two physical partitions while others sit nearly idle

The container's provisioned 10,000 RU/s is split across physical partitions, so the hot partition hits its own local RU/s ceiling and throws 429s even though the container-wide average is only 40% — the average hides the per-partition skew

The partition key is immutable once the container is created — fixing it requires creating a new container with a different partition key and migrating all the data, making a wrong partition key choice very expensive
Fix: choose a partition key with higher cardinality and more even access, e.g. /customerId, or a composite key like country_customerId if country-level grouping is still needed
Country-based filtering is not lost — it becomes a cross-partition query (WHERE country = X) or a country field used for filtering, just no longer the partition key itself

Trade-off: cross-partition queries cost more RU than single-partition queries, so if the app runs frequent whole-country aggregate reports, switching the partition key raises RU cost for those queries — must weigh against actual query patterns; higher cardinality is not automatically better

`throughput` and `autoscale_settings` are two mutually exclusive RU/s provisioning modes on a Cosmos container — the azurerm provider rejects having both set at once because a container can only run one mode at a time.

The diff's error is a leftover config issue: the PR intends to switch to autoscale, but the old manual `throughput = 400` line was never removed when `autoscale_settings` was added — it's stale leftover, not an intentional extra parameter.
Fix: delete the `throughput = 400` line entirely and keep only the `autoscale_settings { max_throughput = 4000 }` block.
Autoscale range mechanics: RU/s automatically flexes between 10% of `max_throughput` and `max_throughput` itself (i.e. 400-4000 RU/s in this case) based on real load.
This directly solves the stated peak-hour spikes problem — RU/s expands and contracts on its own with real traffic, with nobody needing to be on call to manually adjust throughput.

Trade-off: autoscale costs roughly 1.5x manual pricing per RU actually used, so it only makes sense when load swings significantly (like peak-hour traffic); steady year-round load is cheaper with fixed manual `throughput`.
After applying the fix, re-run `terraform plan` to confirm the constraint error is gone before merging.
Nguyên nhân trực tiếp là `eviction_policy = "AllKeysLRU"` đang áp dụng cho TOÀN BỘ database dùng chung, không phân biệt cache hay session.

AllKeysLRU evict theo least-recently-used BẤT KỂ key có TTL hay không — nên một session không có TTL (đúng thiết kế, phải sống hết vòng đời đăng nhập) vẫn nằm trong diện bị evict như một cache key bình thường.

Cơ chế cụ thể gây ra hiện tượng logout bất ngờ: một session bị bỏ quên (user để tab idle, ít được truy cập gần đây) trở thành ứng viên LRU và bị quét mất dù CHƯA hết hạn về mặt logic — đây là evict-vì-ít-dùng chứ không phải expire-vì-hết-TTL.
Sự cố rộ lên đúng giờ cao điểm vì lượng ghi cache tăng vọt → bộ nhớ đầy nhanh hơn → eviction diễn ra thường xuyên/mạnh tay hơn → xác suất một session xui rủi bị quét trúng cũng tăng theo.

Đây là lỗi KIẾN TRÚC chứ không phải bug của Redis: dùng chung một database/policy cho hai loại dữ liệu có SLA độ bền khác nhau (cache = mất được và tính lại được, session = mất là gây hậu quả thật) mới là gốc rễ; chỉnh một tham số trên database dùng chung không giải quyết triệt để.

Giải pháp kiến trúc: tách cache và session thành hai database (hoặc hai instance nếu cần cô lập tài nguyên/scale độc lập) Redis riêng biệt, mỗi bên set eviction_policy khác nhau — cache giữ nguyên AllKeysLRU, session chuyển sang NoEviction để khi đầy bộ nhớ Redis TỪ CHỐI GHI (phát hiện được qua log/alert) thay vì âm thầm evict session cũ.

Tối ưu chi phí đi kèm: right-size riêng theo từng workload nếu tách instance (session cần RAM ít hơn vì bị chặn trên bởi số user online nên sku_name nhỏ là đủ, cache có thể cần scale lớn hơn hoặc class ComputeOptimized/MemoryOptimized) — tách ra vừa thường rẻ hơn dùng chung một instance lớn, vừa loại bỏ rủi ro một workload cướp tài nguyên của workload còn lại.
Add `versioning_enabled = true` inside the `blob_properties` block of the storage account resource.
Add `delete_retention_policy { days = 30 }` (soft delete for blobs) inside the same `blob_properties` block.
The storage account resource correctly references the existing resource group (`azurerm_resource_group.lab.name` / `azurerm_resource_group.lab.location`) rather than redefining it.
Versioning protects against overwrites: each time a blob is overwritten a new version is created, so the original content is not lost and can be recovered by restoring the prior version.
Soft delete protects against outright deletion: a deleted blob/container isn't removed immediately but is kept in a recoverable state for the retention period (30 days) before being permanently gone.
The incident described in the prompt — a script overwriting blobs and losing their content — is specifically the failure mode that versioning solves, not soft delete.

Versioning and soft delete address different failure modes (overwrite vs. delete) and complement rather than duplicate each other, so enabling both together is the production standard since you can't know in advance which type of incident will happen next.

Confirms the PM's concern is real under weak consistency (Eventual/ConsistentPrefix): because of replication lag between the write region and the read region, the user could read the OLD balance right after hitting F5.
Rejects account-wide Strong consistency partly because it forces the highest latency, since it must wait for the write to be replicated/confirmed at the replica before returning a response.
Rejects account-wide Strong consistency also because it does not support multi-region write, making it too heavy an architectural fix just for this balance-display use case.
Identifies Session as the correct consistency level for this use case, noting it is Cosmos DB's recommended default.

Explains that Session provides read-your-writes: a request carrying the same session token as the transfer is guaranteed to see that user's own latest write, regardless of which region (Write or Read) it is served from.

Notes the read-your-writes guarantee is per-session/per-user, not global — different users may still observe eventual consistency between each other, but that is outside what the PM's scenario actually requires.
States the correct scope of application: set Session as the Cosmos account's default consistency level, with no need to override per-request or to force a global Strong setting.

Role definition answers "what can be done": it's a list of `actions` (control-plane operations like creating/deleting/reading resources) and `dataActions` (data-plane operations like reading blob contents, reading a secret), using either a built-in role (Contributor/Reader) or a custom-written one.
The definition alone grants NOBODY any permission — it's just a "permission template" waiting to be used.

Role assignment is what actually grants permission: it's a pairing of THREE pieces — a principal (who: user/group/service principal/managed identity, from Entra ID), a role definition (what: e.g. Contributor), and a scope (where: a specific point in the Management Group → Subscription → Resource Group → Resource tree).

The statement "gave user A Contributor" is missing the single most important piece — WHAT SCOPE? Without it, nobody knows whether user A has Contributor across the entire subscription (very broad) or just on one specific Resource Group (much closer to least-privilege) — a huge difference in risk level.

Keeping the two concepts separate matters because a definition is reusable across countless different assignments, with no need to redefine "what Contributor means" every time it's assigned to someone — this reusability is also what lets an organization standardize permissions consistently.
Separation also makes RBAC easier to audit — you can list every assignment (who, what permission, where) independently of re-understanding what each role means each time.
